messages.subject: AICc vs. likelihood ratio
parts:
Hi All,

I have two questions regarding using AICc for the selection of occuRN models.

1) When comparing models using AICc should I also be calculating new values for AIC weight, cumlative weight and delta, as is done when I do AIC model comparisons using modsel? Or are the values I calculate for AIC weight, cumlative weight and delta when doing AIC model comparisons also applicable for AICc? Is anyone able to suggest how I might produce these values if I in fact need to do this?  

2) My AICc values contradict my likelihood ratio test values, which values do I use? I have calculated AICc values for models 4, 5 and 6. Both model 4, with ki.mainalnd and camera as covariates, and model 6 with just ki.mainalnd as a covariate, have approximately equivalent AICc values (less than 2 points). in this case one should chose the model with the least parameters, this is model 6 with only ki.mainalnd included. However, to make things more confusing the likelihood ratio tests for model 4 vs 5 and model 4 vs 6 suggest that having ki.mainland and camera in the same model is better than just having ki.mainland or just camera. this contradicts the AICc values

I include example code below. Thanks in advance. Pat.

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: AICc vs. likelihood ratio
parts:
I recommend the sidebars in the gentle intro to MARK (ch. 4) as a quick read about IC and LRT: AIC will select the same models as the LRT at a very specific alpha (greater than 0.05 when few parameters are in a model, but declines in a decelerating fashion as K increases).  AICc induces a stronger penalty on model complexity than AIC because the cost of an additional parameter increases with small sample size. Defining n is not always straight-forward for many models, or n may differ for different parameters (the MacKenzie et al. 2006 book talks about this). The choice of some IC or regularization technique for choosing a model or ranking models is the practitioner's decision (you might prefer LASSO, BIC, etc.).  A broader question is whether you are fine with using the most supported model or have some desire to account for uncertainty in the selection of the most supported model and model average (appropriately! see Cade 2015): AIC(c) allows this; the LRT does not. 

All results presented suggest m4 is the 'best' or 'most supported' model out of the ones presented. Your certainty in m4 as the best is a subjective decision that is similar to choosing alpha = 0.10, or 0.05, or 0.00001, or other value.  You have to decide to accept some risk that you are wrong in one way vs. another.

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: AICc vs. likelihood ratio
parts:
*(rather than 'subjective', I should have said something more like "a decision made with some logical justification"). 

-- My interpretation of this situation is that whilst camera does explain explain some variation in my model it does not explain a great deal, would this be correct?

If you're interested in changes in the absolute fit, including the 3 additional parameters associated with camera (vs. just the abundance covariate) decreases the -2 * the log likelihood by about 11.  I don't know how to state this result for this model structure in terms of an R^2 type of metric, or how to practically say that this is a lot of variance or just a little variance being explained, but maybe you can find a reference. The purpose of an IC is to provide a measure of whether fit improvements associated with more complex models outweigh the increases in estimate variance associated with more complex models, and they try to do this by penalizing more complex models in varied ways. The weight of the separate models relates to certainty in the model selection process. Maybe the interpretation is that the improvement in model fit associated with camera moderately (AICc) or more heavily (AIC) outweighs the added complexity/increase in estimate variance associated with including these additional terms, but web of science or google scholar will provide more reliable information than 'tired internet non-statistician paraphrasing his interpretation of references'.
